name: Mirtazapine
lead: Mirtazapine is a tetracyclic antidepressant, usually classed as a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA) and sold under the brand name Remeron among many others; the US label lists major depressive disorder in adults as its indication [1][2][29]. Wikipedia notes that evidence for the NaSSA label is considered weak [29].

It enters appearance and training discussions through two of its common effects: sedation and increased appetite. People discussing it in training forums describe a prescribed bedtime dose helping them sleep during stressful or insomnia-prone periods, and sleep is the link to recovery, training consistency and a rested look; the appetite effect is relevant to people who struggle to eat enough. Wikipedia lists insomnia, low appetite or underweight, anxiety disorders, PTSD, nausea and itching among off-label uses with some supporting evidence [29].

Mirtazapine was synthesised at Organon, approved in the Netherlands in 1994 and introduced in the United States in 1996, and its US patent expired in 2004, after which generics became widely available; Wikipedia reports it was the 99th most prescribed drug in the US in 2023, with more than 6 million prescriptions [29].

Randomized trials have tested it for insomnia in older adults and for appetite in advanced lung cancer, and meta-analyses have examined antidepressant-related weight change [11][12][13][17]. No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes. The label carries a boxed warning about suicidal thoughts and behaviors in young people and lists agranulocytosis, serotonin syndrome, angle-closure glaucoma and QT prolongation among warnings [2].

paras: Grokipedia reports FDA approval on 14 June 1996 for major depressive disorder, based on placebo-controlled six-week trials [1]. The label lists only that indication and states it is not approved for pediatric patients [2]. Network meta-analyses comparing antidepressants include mirtazapine among the drugs ranked for efficacy and acceptability [3][4]. A 2011 Cochrane review described in Grokipedia found faster onset than SSRIs at two weeks [1].
Off-label uses described include insomnia, PTSD, panic disorder, OCD, generalized anxiety and appetite stimulation [1].

A 2011 Cochrane review found faster onset at two weeks among responders but similar efficacy to other antidepressants by six weeks [29]. In 2010 NICE recommended generic SSRIs as first-line, noting mirtazapine had no clear efficacy advantage but that patients were less likely to stop it because of side effects [29]. It is often used when depression comes with anxiety or insomnia, and effects may appear within one to two weeks but can take up to four [29].

The label says the mechanism is unclear but may involve antagonism of central presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors and heteroreceptors, enhancing noradrenergic and serotonergic activity [2]. Grokipedia adds blockade of 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, 5-HT3 and histamine H1 receptors, with H1 blockade contributing to sedation [1].

It does not inhibit reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine or dopamine, nor monoamine oxidase [29]. Its strongest binding is at the histamine H1 receptor, a very potent antihistamine action, followed by 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, 5-HT3 and alpha-2 receptors [29]. Wikipedia describes a sedation paradox: at lower doses strong H1 and serotonin-receptor blockade produces sleepiness, while at higher doses alpha-2 effects offset part of the H1 blockade and sedation can lessen [29].

Oral bioavailability is about 50% and plasma protein binding about 85%; elimination half-life is 20-40 hours; excretion is about 75% in urine and 15% in faeces [29]. The active metabolite desmethylmirtazapine contributes a small share of effect, with a half-life of about 25 hours [29]. Metabolism runs mainly through CYP1A2, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, so fluvoxamine can raise levels markedly and carbamazepine lowers them [29]. The drug is a racemic mixture of two enantiomers; the (S) form, esmirtazapine, was developed separately and studied in insomnia extension trials [9][29]. Chemically it is a piperazinoazepine related to mianserin [29].

Grokipedia reports drowsiness in up to 54 percent of users, weight gain or increased appetite in 12-17 percent, dry mouth, constipation and raised cholesterol [1]. The label lists suicidality warnings, agranulocytosis, serotonin syndrome, angle-closure glaucoma and QT prolongation [2]. A 2011 cohort study examined antidepressant use and adverse outcomes in older people [5].

A 2010 meta-analysis of 116 studies of antidepressants and body weight examined how much weight change different antidepressants produce, noting that results had been sparse and contradictory [13]. A pediatric meta-analysis in JAMA examined suicidal ideation and attempts in young people treated with antidepressants, which underlies the boxed warning [14]. Reviews of newer antidepressants describe their safety and tolerability profiles [15], and a 2010 meta-analysis examined heart-rate variability changes with antidepressants [16].

Compared with other antidepressants, Wikipedia reports more weight gain and sleepiness, less nausea and sexual dysfunction than SSRIs, and very common effects (10% or more) of constipation, dry mouth, sleepiness, increased appetite (about 17%) and weight gain [29]. Restless legs syndrome was reported in 8-28% of people in a 2012 review, and rare REM sleep behavior disorder has occurred [29]. Stopping abruptly may cause anxiety, dizziness, irritability, insomnia and flu-like symptoms, and gradual reduction is the usual guidance [29]. Mirtazapine is considered relatively safe in overdose, with a fatal toxicity index of 3.1 deaths per million prescriptions, similar to SSRIs [29]. Combining with MAOIs requires a two-week gap in either direction [29].

For sleep, the MIRAGE trial randomized 60 adults aged 65 and older with chronic insomnia to a low dose of mirtazapine or placebo for 28 days. The Insomnia Severity Index fell by 6.5 points with mirtazapine versus 2.9 with placebo (p=0.003); there were no severe adverse events, and 6 mirtazapine participants versus 1 placebo participant stopped treatment because of adverse events [11]. The DREAMING trial tested low-dose mirtazapine and amitriptyline against placebo in general-practice patients with insomnia and sleep-maintenance problems [12].

For appetite, a randomized, double-blind trial in 86 patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer compared mirtazapine with placebo for 8 weeks, assessing appetite on the Anorexia Cachexia Scale and energy intake, with all patients receiving dietary advice [17]. Registered trials examined cancer patients losing more than 10 percent of their body weight (terminated, n=13) [8] and short-term metabolic effects in healthy volunteers [18].

Mirtazapine is marketed under a very large number of brand names worldwide, and generics have been available since the 2004 US patent expiry [29]. Musician Hayley Williams wrote a song titled "Mirtazapine" about her experience with the drug, released on her 2025 album Ego Death at a Bachelorette Party [29]. It is also used in cats and dogs as an appetite stimulant [29].

Wikipedia reports mixed or negative findings for several explored uses: it is ineffective for sleep apnea, and a trial of breathlessness in COPD or interstitial lung disease (BETTER-B) found it ineffective and potentially harmful; it has also been explored for autism-related symptoms, akathisia and drug withdrawal [29]. Registered and recent trials include methamphetamine use disorder [20], hyperemesis gravidarum [21] and functional dyspepsia [6].

On T Nation, mirtazapine comes up in testosterone-therapy and training logs. A poster in a thread on insomnia after starting TRT described raising mirtazapine to a more antidepressant-range dose and treating low testosterone and depression or anxiety as separate problems [25]. A log describes a prescription for mirtazapine for sleep and anxiety linked to gastrointestinal problems [26], and another poster described mirtazapine as the one prescribed drug that helped sleep without side effects, in contrast to benzodiazepines [27]. A recovery log listed it among pharmaceuticals the author was willing to consider for dopamine-related symptoms [28].

Large network meta-analyses compared 21 and 12 antidepressants for acute major depression [3][4]. Registered trials include small studies on mirtazapine in functional dyspepsia, weight gain, sleep disorders in Alzheimer's disease and cancer-related weight loss, and extension trials of its enantiomer esmirtazapine in insomnia [6][7][8][9]. No studies were found testing mirtazapine for appearance outcomes.

A pharmacogenetic trial examined a leptin-receptor polymorphism and mirtazapine weight gain in late-life depression (n=19) [19]. Other recent randomized work includes a 2026 phase 3 trial in 339 adults with methamphetamine use disorder in Australia [20] and a randomized trial comparing mirtazapine or ondansetron for hyperemesis gravidarum [21]. Network meta-analyses have also placed it among augmentation options for treatment-resistant depression and among drugs for generalised anxiety disorder [22][23]. The STAR*D study rationale describes the sequenced-treatment design in which mirtazapine was one option [24].

timeline.event: FDA approves mirtazapine for major depressive disorder; introduced as Remeron [1][29].
NICE recommends generic SSRIs first-line; meta-analysis of 116 studies on antidepressants and weight published [13][29].
Cochrane review reports faster onset than comparators at two weeks [29].
99th most prescribed drug in the US with over 6 million prescriptions [29].
MIRAGE trial of low-dose mirtazapine for chronic insomnia in older adults published [11].

lore.intro: Among lifters on T Nation, mirtazapine is described as a prescribed sleep and mood drug used alongside TRT, rather than as an appearance product [25][26][27].

claims.claim: Mirtazapine helps sleep when other options fail
claims.believers: Posters report that a prescribed bedtime dose helped them sleep during insomnia on testosterone therapy or GI-related sleep problems [25][26][27].
claims.experts: The MIRAGE trial in 60 older adults found a larger ISI improvement than placebo over 28 days [11]; the label lists only major depressive disorder as its indication [2].

claims.claim: It causes weight gain and increases appetite
claims.believers: Users describe the sedating and appetite effects as defining features of the drug.
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports weight gain or increased appetite in 12-17 percent of users, a meta-analysis of 116 studies examined antidepressant weight change, and a lung-cancer trial tested it for appetite [1][13][17].

claims.claim: A bedtime dose helps recovery by fixing sleep
claims.believers: Lifters on T Nation link better sleep on a prescribed bedtime dose to staying consistent with training [25][27].
claims.experts: The MIRAGE trial reported larger insomnia-score improvement than placebo in older adults over 28 days; no trial has tested training or physique outcomes [11].

claims.claim: Its appetite effect can help people gain weight
claims.believers: Posters describe the appetite and sedation effects as defining features [27].
claims.experts: A lung-cancer trial tested it for appetite and a 116-study meta-analysis examined antidepressant weight change; Wikipedia reports about 17% increased appetite [13][17][29].

claims.claim: Sedation is strongest at lower doses
claims.believers: Users commonly describe it as a sleep drug rather than an antidepressant.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes a dose-response paradox in which sedation is stronger at lower doses because H1 blockade is partly offset by alpha-2 effects at higher doses [29].

claims.claim: It is easy to stop whenever wanted
claims.believers: Some forum posters treat it as a short-term sleep aid.
claims.experts: Withdrawal symptoms can occur on abrupt discontinuation, and a gradual reduction is recommended [29].

card.summary: A sedating, appetite-boosting prescription antidepressant sometimes used off-label for sleep; approved for depression, untested for looks.
card.note: Boxed warning for suicidality in young people; weight gain and heavy sedation are common.

quick.overview:
Mirtazapine is a prescription antidepressant approved in the US for major depressive disorder in adults. Its sedating and appetite-increasing effects lead to off-label use for insomnia and appetite loss.

No published trial has tested it for appearance goals, and the wiki found no community discussion to cite.
quick.mechanism: It is thought to block presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, raising noradrenergic and serotonergic activity, and also blocks several serotonin receptors and histamine H1, which is linked to sedation.
quick.risks: Reported effects include drowsiness, weight gain, dry mouth, constipation and raised cholesterol. The label has a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts in young people and lists agranulocytosis, serotonin syndrome and QT prolongation. Prescription-only.

chain: Sleepiness and deeper sleep; appetite rises
Better sleep supports recovery and training; higher intake can support weight gain
angle.text: Mirtazapine is a prescription drug whose sedating and appetite-raising effects are sometimes used by prescribers for insomnia and poor appetite. Forum members describe it as a sleep aid during hard training or testosterone-therapy periods, and the weight-gain effect is a documented consequence rather than an appearance claim.
